### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Ambali, Jung, and Sorensen link the 2015 New York State Building Condition Survey — engineer- or architect-led inspections that state law requires for every occupied public school building — to enrollment and district-finance data for roughly 2,350 traditional public schools outside New York City, and document large, item-specific racial gaps in the realized physical condition of schools. That descriptive core is the paper's contribution and it is trustworthy: relative to schools more than 80% White, schools more than 50% non-White are 25.9 percentage points less likely to have a satisfactory ventilation system, 20.0 points less likely to have satisfactory humidity, 17.3 points less likely to have a good appearance rating, 14.6 points less likely to be rated clean, 19.4 points less likely to have athletic fields, 11.5 points less likely to have a health office, and 7.1 points more likely to have mold (Table 1), and the student-weighted exposure analysis shows that Hispanic students (−0.32 SD on the overall index) and Black students (−0.19 SD) bear these gaps while Asian, multiracial, American Indian/Alaska Native, and White students attend above-average buildings (Figure 2). These numbers are internally consistent — Figure 1 reproduces the pooled Table 1 means, the index rows are exact averages of their items, and the text quotes the tables accurately with one swap — and they are large enough to survive the district-level clustering the paper does not do. The field should be far more careful with the second half of the paper, which is what the abstract leads with and what policy audiences will quote. The Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition (Table 2, Figure 3) is arithmetically faithful — property taxes' 30%, donations' 7%, and state building aid's −17% recompute exactly as E + C + I for each covariate over the 0.0830 gap — but Table 2 omits the constant term, and the listed covariate coefficient rows sum to about −0.010 against a reported coefficients component of 0.0603, so roughly 0.070 (84% of the overall gap; more than the entire gap for the aesthetics and environmental indices) sits in an unreported intercept difference that neither the table nor Figure 3 shows. The paper's reading of the large coefficients component as evidence that funding channels "have different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" (p. 8) therefore attributes to the covariates a quantity that is almost entirely the unexplained residual. The per-covariate "percent explained" bars also mix an invariant endowment piece with coefficient and interaction pieces that depend on where each variable's zero sits — and the interaction-to-coefficient ratios in Table 2 (−2.17 for property taxes in all four columns) imply the continuous finance variables were centered in a way the paper never reports. On the invariant endowment piece alone, property-tax differences account for 51% of the gap under the paper's non-White-coefficient reference and 12% under the White-coefficient reference; state aid for −13% and −31%; donations for a non-significant 2%. Add robust rather than district-clustered standard errors on district-level finance regressors, causal language ("successfully helping to equalize," p. 11; "helps reduce these disparities," abstract) that contradicts the authors' own p. 5 caveat, the mechanical link between reimbursement-style building aid and recent construction, two Table 1 significance markers the reported means and cell sizes cannot produce, and an analytic sample that is 2,352 in the text, 2,371 in Table 1, and 1,440 rather than 1,459 in Table 2, and the right posture is: cite the paper for the existence, size, and item profile of inspection-based racial gaps in school facilities in New York outside NYC as of 2015, and for the student-weighted incidence on Hispanic and Black students; treat the finance decomposition as a directional association (local property-tax capacity lines up with the gap, state building aid lines up against it) rather than as the specific percentages or the policy verdicts the abstract offers.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The arithmetic here is right; the charge that the paper misreads it is withdrawn. Table 2 prints no constant row, and the overall-index coefficient rows do sum to −0.0095 against the reported 0.0603, so about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap) sits in the unprinted Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder intercept. But the 30% recomputes exactly ((0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%), every Figure 3 bar recomputes from Table 2, and the paper never claims that the listed covariates account for the whole gap. This is a reporting omission (no constant row, so a reader cannot check the total) rather than a text–table discrepancy, and it was removed from the audit's list of errors after a blind second reading. The advice to describe property taxes as the largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain remains sound; the description of the paper's reading as an error does not. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed by recomputation from the rendered table.

#### Key Strengths

- The outcome is realized building condition from a statutory, professionally conducted inspection census — 2,473 of 2,875 traditional public schools outside NYC (86%), the last full-census wave before the BCS moved to annual samples of 500–560 schools — not dollars spent. Moving from capital outlay (Brunner et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022) to the ventilation, humidity, mold, and facility access students actually experience is the paper's clearest conceptual contribution and fills a genuine gap.
- The descriptive exhibits are item-level, large, and internally consistent. Twenty-four items across three domains are reported by school racial composition with means and tests (Table 1); the index rows are exact averages of their items; Figure 1 matches the pooled Table 1 means to two decimals on every item; and the gaps on the dimensions the mechanism literature cares most about (ventilation −25.9 pp, humidity −20.0 pp, mold +7.1 pp, health office −11.5 pp, all p < .01) are too large for clustering or rater effects to erase.
- The student-weighted exposure analysis (Figure 2) unbundles the coarse ">50% non-White" category and shows that the disadvantage falls specifically on Hispanic (−0.32 SD overall) and Black (−0.19 SD) students, while Asian (+0.05), multiracial (+0.10), AIAN (+0.15), and White (+0.21) students attend above-average buildings. All 24 cell values quoted in the text match the rendered figure. This is the paper's most distinctive and citable exhibit.
- The decomposition is fully reported and fully recomputable: the threefold equations are written out with the non-White coefficients as reference (p. 4); Table 2 gives all twelve covariates' endowment, coefficient, and interaction terms with SEs for all four indices; E + C + I equals the gap in every column; and every bar in Figure 3 (30% property taxes, 7% donations, −17% state aid, and the smaller ones) recomputes exactly from Table 2.
- The authors state the limits plainly where it counts: the decomposition "remains descriptive and could contain bias due to omitted variables or reverse causality" and "does not establish causal relationships" (p. 5); the data are one cross-section; the items may be subjective (p. 12). The literature review's typology of the capital-spending evidence (null / delayed / strong) is fair and does not cherry-pick, and citation integrity is clean (all 52 references cited; no dangling in-text citations).

#### Key Concerns

- Most of the decomposed gap is in an unreported intercept, and the text reads it as a covariate result. Table 2's detailed endowment and interaction rows sum to their totals, but the coefficient rows sum to about −0.0095 for the overall index against a reported coefficients component of 0.0603; the implied constant is about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap), about 0.093 for aesthetics (105% of that gap), 0.091 for environment (151%), and 0.026 for health/recreation. Figure 3 shows no bar for it, so all twelve covariate bars together net to roughly 16% of the overall gap while the property-tax bar alone reads 30%. The p. 8 sentence attributing the large coefficients component to funding channels having "different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" is not what the listed rows show; across the covariates, the coefficient differences net to zero or slightly negative.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The arithmetic here is right; the charge that the paper misreads it is withdrawn. Table 2 prints no constant row, and the overall-index coefficient rows do sum to −0.0095 against the reported 0.0603, so about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap) sits in the unprinted Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder intercept. But the 30% recomputes exactly ((0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%), every Figure 3 bar recomputes from Table 2, and the paper never claims that the listed covariates account for the whole gap. This is a reporting omission (no constant row, so a reader cannot check the total) rather than a text–table discrepancy, and it was removed from the audit's list of errors after a blind second reading. The advice to describe property taxes as the largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain remains sound; the description of the paper's reading as an error does not. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed by recomputation from the rendered table.

- The per-covariate percentages depend on unreported normalization choices. Under the p. 4 equations, I_k/C_k = (X̄_W − X̄_NW)/X̄_NW, which is constant across outcome columns for each covariate (it is: −2.17 for property taxes, about −1.30 for state aid, −1.44 federal aid, −1.24 bonds, −2.0 enrollment) and implies opposite-signed group means for every continuous variable — impossible for raw per-pupil dollars or enrollment, so those variables were centered or standardized without disclosure, while the locale and school-level dummies (same-sign ratios) were not. Coefficient and interaction contributions are not invariant to such shifts (Oaxaca & Ransom, 1999; Jann, 2008), reference categories for the dummies are never stated, and the "pp = thousands of dollars per pupil" note is at best incomplete. The invariant endowment shares tell a more modest story: property taxes 51% (or 12% with White coefficients as reference), state aid −13% (−31%), donations 2% and not significant.
- Causal wording outruns the descriptive design, especially for state building aid and donations. The abstract says aid "helps reduce these disparities," the introduction that it "meaningfully narrows infrastructure gaps," and the Results that the progressive formula "is successfully helping to equalize gaps" (p. 11), against the authors' own p. 5 caveat. New York building aid reimburses approved capital projects, so districts that recently built receive more aid per pupil and have better-rated buildings; the association is what one would see even if the formula equalized nothing, and the state-aid contribution flips sign (+0.0057) for the health/recreation index. The donations claim ("contribute meaningfully," p. 12) rests entirely on the location-dependent coefficient term (0.0056); the endowment (0.0020, SE 0.0012) is not significant and E + I ≈ 0 in every column, implying β_W ≈ 0.
- Inference ignores the district structure, and two Table 1 stars cannot be right. Finance covariates are district-level comptroller data assigned to every school in a district, and each district hires its own inspection firm (so rater standards are district-level too), yet Table 2 reports robust, unclustered SEs and Table 1 uses simple two-group t-tests; the number of districts is never reported. Separately, swimming pool (0.152 vs 0.119, n = 940/519) is marked ** and the text repeats p < .01, but a two-proportion test gives t ≈ 1.8 (p ≈ .07); stadium condition (0.386 vs 0.162) is marked * but gives t ≈ 9.9. The other 22 rows reproduce. The cluster unit for the Figure 2 bootstrap is also unstated.
- The prose and exhibits disagree in several places a reader could be caught by, and nothing can be verified outside the article. Page 5 says "85% have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating" — Figure 1a and the pooled Table 1 means show the reverse (appearance 0.85, lighting 0.75). The abstract lists gymnasiums among "significantly" reduced-access facilities (the gap is −0.025 at p < .1). The introduction describes the comparison group as "predominantly Black and Hispanic" when it is >50% non-White of any group. The analytic sample is 2,352 (text) but 2,371 (Table 1), and Table 2's N of 1,440 is 19 short of the 940 + 519 it compares; neither is explained. The "condition satisfactory" items are unconditional shares, so the athletic-field and stadium "condition" gaps largely restate presence gaps (conditional on having the facility, the satisfactory share is 0.889 W vs 0.913 NW for fields, 0.902 vs 0.895 for stadiums). There is no data-availability statement, no code, no software version, no access pathway for the NYSED-provided BCS file, and the poverty/locale comparisons, Figure 2 significance tests, Model 1–3 sensitivity, and latent-factor check live only in an online supplement not bundled with the PDF.

#### What to Rely On

- Large racial gaps in inspected building conditions exist in New York outside NYC as of 2015, on the dimensions that matter most for health and learning: relative to mostly-White schools, mostly-non-White schools are 25.9 pp less likely to have a satisfactory ventilation system, 20.0 pp less likely to have satisfactory humidity, 7.1 pp more likely to have mold, 17.3 pp less likely to have a good appearance rating, 14.6 pp less likely to be rated clean, and 8.1 pp less likely to be rated satisfactory overall (Table 1, all p < .01). Quote these from Table 1, not from the introduction's rounded versions.
- Access gaps in health and recreational facilities: mostly-non-White schools are 19.4 pp less likely to have athletic fields, 24.7 pp less likely to have an external stadium, and 11.5 pp less likely to have a health office in the building (Table 1, p < .01). Treat these as gaps in having the facility, not in its upkeep.
- The incidence falls on Hispanic and Black students specifically. Student-weighted, Hispanic students attend schools 0.32 SD below the mean on the overall index (−0.25 aesthetics, −0.24 environment, −0.16 recreation/health) and Black students 0.19 SD below (−0.16, −0.03, −0.19); Asian, multiracial, AIAN, and White students are at +0.05 to +0.21 (Figure 2). Note the SD unit is the student-weighted cross-school SD of each index, standardized separately, so do not compare magnitudes across columns.
- The overall condition of the stock: 84% of schools rated satisfactory overall, only 49% with central HVAC, 67% with satisfactory ventilation, 62% with satisfactory humidity, 92% mold-free, 68% with a playground, 32% with an external stadium, 13% with a pool, 90% with a health office (Figure 1; all verified against pooled Table 1 means).
- A directional finance association that holds across all four indices and under either reference group: differences in per-pupil local property-tax revenue are positively and significantly associated with the White/non-White gap (endowment terms 0.0425, 0.0583, 0.0254, 0.0437, all p < .01), and differences in state building aid are negatively associated with it for three of four indices (endowments −0.0107, −0.0257, −0.0100; the health/recreation term is +0.0036, n.s.). The paper reports that the property-tax share attenuates to roughly 20% once taxable property values and other community covariates enter (Model 3), consistent with property-tax revenue proxying local fiscal capacity — but that check is appendix-only.
- The paper's own framing of what it is: descriptive, cross-sectional, non-causal (pp. 5, 12).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Local property taxes are the largest contributor to racial gaps" / "explain 30%" / "nearly one-third" — the 30% is E + C + I for one covariate over a gap of which about 84% sits in an unreported constant; the twelve covariates together net to about 16%. The invariant endowment share is 51% under the paper's reference group and 12% under the other. Say "largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain," and give a range rather than a point.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The arithmetic here is right; the charge that the paper misreads it is withdrawn. Table 2 prints no constant row, and the overall-index coefficient rows do sum to −0.0095 against the reported 0.0603, so about 0.070 (84% of the 0.0830 gap) sits in the unprinted Kitagawa–Oaxaca–Blinder intercept. But the 30% recomputes exactly ((0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%), every Figure 3 bar recomputes from Table 2, and the paper never claims that the listed covariates account for the whole gap. This is a reporting omission (no constant row, so a reader cannot check the total) rather than a text–table discrepancy, and it was removed from the audit's list of errors after a blind second reading. The advice to describe property taxes as the largest identified contributor to a gap the model mostly does not explain remains sound; the description of the paper's reading as an error does not. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed by recomputation from the rendered table.

- "State building aid helps reduce these disparities" / "is successfully helping to equalize gaps" — a counterfactual claim from a descriptive decomposition; only the endowment piece (−0.0107, p < .05) is significant, the −17% combines it with two non-significant terms, the sign flips for the health/recreation index, and reimbursement-style aid mechanically tracks recent construction. Read as: districts serving more students of color receive more building aid per pupil, and aid is positively associated with conditions.
- "Donations contribute meaningfully to the observed racial gaps" — the 7% comes entirely from the location-dependent coefficient term; the endowment (0.0020) is not significant and E + I ≈ 0, so the "White communities use wealth to donate" story is not supported by the invariant components.
- The p. 8 interpretation of the coefficients component as covariates having "different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" — the covariate coefficient rows sum to −0.0095 (overall), −0.0047 (aesthetics), −0.0428 (environment); the positive total is the intercept. The same paragraph's "for most indices" understates: C > E in all four.
- Any Table 2 or Figure 3 percentage as a stable number — the continuous covariates appear centered without disclosure, omitted categories are unstated, and no `oaxaca` normalization options are reported; C and I terms move with those choices.
- Every significance star on a marginal item — SEs are robust, not district-clustered, on district-level regressors and district-run inspections; the number of districts is unreported. Treat vermin (+), heating (+), gymnasium (+), cooling satisfactory (*), and playground condition (*) as unresolved, and note that swimming pool (**) and stadium condition (*) carry stars the reported means and Ns cannot produce.
- "Athletic fields and external stadiums are also in worse condition" (pp. 2, 7) — the condition items are unconditional, and conditional on presence the satisfactory shares are equal or higher in mostly-non-White schools; these are presence gaps. The health/recreation index (the largest gap, 0.100) also counts presence twice for these items and weights stadiums and pools — amenities — equally with health offices.
- The p. 5 sentence "85% have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating" — reversed; use Figure 1a (appearance 85%, lighting 75%). The introduction's "25 percentage points" for ventilation is 25.9 in Table 1. The abstract's "gymnasiums" is a −2.5 pp gap at p < .1.
- "Schools serving predominantly Black and Hispanic students" (p. 2) — the comparison group is >50% non-White of any group, pooling predominantly Asian suburban schools with high-poverty urban Black and Hispanic schools that Figure 2 shows have very different conditions; use Figure 2 for group-specific statements.
- "New York State" — New York City is excluded (note 2), the title and abstract do not say so, and NYC enrolls a large share of the state's Black and Hispanic students; the data are a single 2015 cross-section, and no comparable statewide census has been collected since.
- The Figure 2 significance statements (including "0.01 SD (p < .005)" and "0.00 SD (p < .05)") — tests against the most advantaged group for each index (which changes by index: AIAN for recreation and environment), from an unspecified cluster bootstrap, with results only in Appendix Table A7.
- The poverty-tier and locale comparisons (p. 8), the Model 1–3 sensitivity check ("roughly 30% to roughly 20%," p. 11), the latent-factor robustness (note 11), the representativeness claim for the 86% sample (note 4), and the index SDs of "0.14 to 0.17" (p. 8) — all rest on the online supplement or on nothing citable in the main text.
- The novelty claim "first comprehensive analysis ... using large-scale building inspection data" — defensible only through its qualifiers. GAO (1995) and NCES (2000) broke facility conditions out by minority enrollment (survey-based), Simons et al. (2010) and Sorensen et al. (2024) already used the New York BCS, and Brunner et al. (2023) is the primary antecedent for the property-wealth mechanism. Cite this paper for inspection-based, student-weighted, item-level gaps in one state, not for discovering that facilities differ by race or that local wealth drives them.
- Several literature characterizations worth checking before repeating: Duncombe & Wang (2009) cited as an outcomes study (it is a descriptive survey of state capital-funding programs); Baron, Hyman & Vasquez (2026) cited for capital-spending heterogeneity (its subject is operating funding and adult crime); Park et al. (2020) cited only for heat effects, without noting that it documents racial disparities in school air conditioning — the opposite of this paper's +3.6 pp cooling result, which the paper attributes to locale using appendix tables only.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper has two parts that deserve different amounts of trust. The descriptive part, which links building-inspection data for about 2,400 schools outside New York City to enrollment and finance data, is credible and internally consistent. It supports the headline claim: schools serving mostly students of color report worse ventilation, humidity, cleanliness, and appearance, and less access to athletic fields and health offices. The Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder (KOB) decomposition that produces the policy headline ("property taxes explain 30%," "donations 7%," "state aid offsets 17%") is much more fragile. Three problems drive this. First, the per-covariate "percent explained" figures mix components that depend on arbitrary choices, and the continuous covariates appear to have been centered in a way the paper never reports. Second, the paper misreads the aggregate "coefficients" component. Third, the standard errors ignore the district-level structure of both the finance variables and the inspection process.

**Strengths:**

- The data source is unusual and valuable: engineer- or architect-led building-condition inspections that state law requires for all occupied public school buildings, covering 2,473 of 2,875 traditional public schools outside NYC (86%; p. 3). The arithmetic checks out: 2,473/2,875 = 0.860, and 2,926 − 51 charter schools = 2,875 (note 4, p. 13).
- [Checkable] The descriptive exhibits agree with each other. The domain means in Table 1 (p. 6) closely match the group means in Table 2 (p. 9). The overall index in Table 2 is exactly the mean of the three domain indices: (0.8977 + 0.8507 + 0.6532)/3 = 0.8005, and (0.8092 + 0.7904 + 0.5529)/3 = 0.7175. Pooling Table 1's group means reproduces Figure 1's shares (e.g., overall condition satisfactory ≈ 0.837 vs. 84%; ventilation ≈ 0.670 vs. 67%).
- [Checkable] The KOB summary rows add up: E + C + I equals the reported gap in all four columns (e.g., overall 0.0337 + 0.0603 − 0.0110 = 0.0830; Table 2, p. 9). The detailed endowment and interaction rows sum to their totals. The equations on p. 4 are the standard threefold decomposition, with the non-White coefficients (β_NW) as the reference for endowments (Jann's default).
- [Checkable] Figure 3's bars (p. 11) can be exactly recovered from Table 2 as E + C + I for each covariate. For example, property taxes: (0.0425 + 0.0151 − 0.0328)/0.0830 = 29.9%. Donations: 6.7%. State building aid: −17.1%. The text's 30%, 7%, and −17% (p. 10) are therefore arithmetically correct under the paper's own construction.
- The student-weighted exposure analysis (Figure 2, p. 7) usefully separates specific groups: Hispanic students fare worst, and they are hidden inside the "mostly non-White" category. The authors state plainly that the decomposition is descriptive (p. 5) and that the data are cross-sectional (p. 12).

**Weaknesses:**

- [Derived from Table 2 + p. 4 equations] **The continuous covariates appear to be centered or transformed in an unreported way, which makes Figure 3's shares depend on that choice.** Under the paper's equations, I_k / C_k = (X̄_W − X̄_NW)/X̄_NW for each covariate. That ratio depends only on covariate means, so it should be the same in all four outcome columns, and it is. For property taxes it is −2.17 in every column. For state building aid it is about −1.30, for federal aid about −1.44, for bonds about −1.24, and for enrollment about −2.0. Each of these implies that the two groups' covariate means have opposite signs, which is impossible for raw per-pupil dollars or raw enrollment. The dummy variables, by contrast, give same-sign ratios, as expected; for example, the implied share of White schools in cities is about 3% of the non-White share. The coefficients and interactions components for each covariate, and so Figure 3's "combined" bars, change when a covariate's zero point shifts. Readers therefore cannot tell how much of the 30% or −17% reflects this unreported normalization. (The only alternative explanation is that Table 2 was not computed with the equations printed on p. 4.)
- [Derived from Table 2] **Figure 3 leaves out the constant, which dominates.** The detailed coefficients rows for the overall index sum to −0.0095, but the reported coefficients total is 0.0603 (p. 9–10). The implied intercept difference, about 0.070, is roughly 84% of the overall gap. Under Figure 3's metric, all twelve covariates together account for only about 16% of the overall gap, so property taxes' 30% is larger than the covariates' net total. For the environmental index, the implied intercept term is about 151% of the gap, and the covariates' combined contribution is net negative (about −50%).

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: a reporting omission, not an error in the paper.*

- [Checkable + interpretive] **The paper misreads the coefficients component.** The text says the large coefficients component suggests that "contributing factors ... have different associations ... in ways that exacerbate inequality" (p. 8). But the covariate-specific coefficient terms sum to a negative number for the overall index (−0.0095), for aesthetics (−0.0047), and for environment (−0.0428). The positive coefficients totals are entirely the intercept, meaning the group difference that none of the covariates capture. Also, the text says the coefficients component is largest "for most indices," but it is larger than endowments in all four columns (Table 2, p. 9).
- [Derived] **The "donations" story is not supported by the location-invariant pieces.** E + I = (X̄_W − X̄_NW)·β_W, which does not depend on where a covariate's zero point sits. For donations it is about zero in every column (overall 0.0020 − 0.0020 = 0.0000; health 0.0043 − 0.0045). That implies β_W ≈ 0. The 7% comes entirely from the location-dependent coefficients term, 0.0056. The endowment itself, 0.0020 (SE 0.0012; p. 9), is not significant. This does not match the interpretation that "White communities may use their access to wealth to donate" (p. 10; repeated on p. 12).
- [Interpretive] **The size of the property-tax and state-aid attributions depends heavily on the reference group.** The location-invariant endowment shares are 51% for property taxes and −13% for state aid with non-White coefficients as the reference (E alone). With White coefficients as the reference (E + I) they are 12% and −31%. The aggregate explained share is 41% versus 27%. The paper reports only one reference group and gives no pooled or alternative-reference decomposition in the main text.
- [Checkable] **The standard errors ignore district clustering.** Table 2 reports "robust standard errors" (p. 10), and the t-tests in Table 1 are simple two-group comparisons (p. 6). Yet the finance covariates are district-level comptroller data (p. 4), and each district runs its own inspection with its own contracted architecture or engineering firm (p. 3). The number of districts, overall and among the 519 mostly non-White schools, is not reported. The effective sample size for the finance coefficients is the number of districts, so the significance stars in Table 2 are probably overstated.
- [Checkable] **Some significance flags in Table 1 cannot be right given the group sizes.** Swimming pool (0.152 vs. 0.119, n = 940/519) is marked ** (p < .01), and the text repeats "p < .01" (p. 7). An unpaired test of two proportions gives SE ≈ 0.018 and p ≈ 0.07. Smaller item-level n would only widen the SE. Conversely, stadium condition (0.386 vs. 0.162) is marked only * (p < .05), but the implied t is about 10. The stars for these two rows look transposed or miscoded.
- [Derived from Table 1] **The "condition" items are unconditional, so condition gaps mostly restate presence gaps.** The condition shares never exceed the presence shares. Among schools that have the facility, the implied share in satisfactory condition is similar or higher in mostly non-White schools: athletic fields 0.913 vs. 0.889, stadium 0.895 vs. 0.902, playground 0.929 vs. 0.883. The claims that these facilities "are in worse condition on average" (p. 2) and "in significantly better condition in predominantly White schools" (p. 7) conflate having a facility with its upkeep. The health/recreation index also counts presence twice for these items.
- [Checkable] Sample sizes are not fully reconciled. The analytic sample is 2,352 schools (p. 4; 1,409 + 369 + 436 + 138 = 2,352), but Table 1's columns sum to 2,371 (940 + 912 + 519; p. 6). Table 2 uses 1,440 observations, while Table 1's two extreme groups total 1,459 (p. 10). Both gaps are 19 schools, so Table 1 appears to use a slightly larger sample than the stated full-coverage sample.
- [Checkable] There is a minor text error on p. 5: "85% have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating." Figure 1a (p. 5) and Table 1 show the reverse: appearance 0.85, lighting 0.75.
- [Interpretive] Measurement. Inspections are done by district-hired teams, so rater effects are tied to districts, and districts in turn are strongly tied to racial composition and finance. Any systematic difference in how urban and rural districts' consultants rate "good" versus "fair" would load directly onto the racial gap. The paper acknowledges that the items "may be subjective" (p. 12) but does not discuss this district-level rater structure. Collapsing Likert scales to binaries is defended with Appendix Table A2 (note 5), which could not be checked.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the item-level descriptive gaps in Table 1 (p. 6) with large magnitudes: ventilation −25.9 pp, humidity −20.0 pp, appearance −17.3 pp, cleanliness −14.6 pp, athletic fields −19.4 pp, health office −11.5 pp, mold +7.1 pp. These are large enough that district clustering is unlikely to erase them. Treat the marginal items (vermin, heating, gymnasium, swimming pool) as unresolved.
- Read the facility "condition" gaps (athletic fields, stadium, playground) as gaps in having the facility, not in its upkeep. Also, stadiums and swimming pools are amenities, and they weigh heavily in the health/recreation index, which has the largest gap (0.100; Table 2).
- Do not quote "property taxes explain 30%" as a stable number. The most defensible statement is directional: the property-tax endowment is positive and significant for all four indices (0.0425, 0.0583, 0.0254, 0.0437; Table 2, p. 9). Its share of the overall gap ranges from roughly 12% to 51% depending on the reference group. Remember that roughly 84% of the overall gap sits in an intercept term that Figure 3 does not show.
- Treat "state building aid narrows the gap" and "gaps would be even larger in the absence of state building aid" (pp. 2, 10–11) as correlational. Building aid reimburses approved capital projects, so it partly marks recent construction rather than formula progressivity. The paper's own caveat about reverse causality (p. 5) applies directly here.
- Set the donations finding aside. Its contribution comes entirely from a location-dependent coefficients term, and the donations endowment is not significant.
- Scope: the results describe New York State outside NYC in 2015, comparing schools that are more than 80% White with schools that are more than 50% non-White. The 912 mixed schools are excluded from the decomposition. The results should not be read as statewide, including NYC, or as current conditions.
- In Figure 2, do not compare magnitudes across columns. Each index is standardized separately, so the overall index's SD-unit values are consistently about 1.5 times the average of its component values (e.g., Hispanic −0.32 overall vs. −0.16/−0.25/−0.24). The "most advantaged group" used as the reference also changes by index: AIAN is highest for recreation/health (0.16) and environment (0.12).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and data.* This is a descriptive study, and its first two research questions (the state of building conditions, and how they differ by race) are well matched to a large administrative inspection census. The 2015 Building Condition Survey is the last full-census wave (p. 3; note 3). Coverage is high, although note 4's claim that the 86% analytic sample shows "no evidence of systematic differences" is asserted without a supporting table in the main text. The main measurement concern is structural rather than about individual items: each district organizes its own inspection team (p. 3), so rater standards vary at the district level, which is also the level at which racial composition and finance vary. A reader cannot rule out that part of the gap in subjective ratings like appearance, lighting, or cleanliness reflects differences in consultants' standards rather than in the buildings themselves. Gaps in more objective items (presence of athletic fields or a health office) are less exposed to this concern. The index construction averages 0/1 items within domains and then averages the three domains. That gives the health/recreation domain, which includes stadiums and pools, one-third of the weight in the overall index. The latent-factor alternative (note 11; RMSEA = .054) and its "closely match" decomposition results (Appendix Tables A11–A12) could not be checked.

*Descriptive inference.* Table 1's t-tests do not account for schools being nested in districts. For the largest gaps this hardly matters, but for items near p = .05–.10 it does. Recomputing unpaired two-proportion tests from the reported means and group n's reproduces most of the stars but not two. Swimming pool (** reported; p ≈ .07 recomputed) and stadium condition (* reported; t ≈ 10 recomputed) look miscoded. The text copies the swimming-pool p < .01 (p. 7). Figure 2 uses a "nonparametric cluster bootstrap" with 200 replications (p. 4) but never names the clustering unit. The significance language on p. 8 is loose: "99% significance level," and a single "p < .005" for a 0.01 SD value. The results of these comparisons depend on which group is the most advantaged, which differs by index. The internal arithmetic of Figure 2 is coherent (the overall index behaves as expected given separate standardization), but the underlying tables (Appendix A7) could not be checked.

*The decomposition.* This is where readers should be most careful, because it produces the abstract's policy conclusions. Four points stand out. (1) The equations on p. 4 are correct, and the summary rows add up. (2) Because C_k and I_k share the factor (β_W − β_NW), the ratio I_k/C_k shows each covariate's relative group means. For five continuous covariates, those ratios imply opposite-signed means, so the variables must have been centered (or otherwise shifted) without disclosure. That matters because the coefficients and interactions components, and hence Figure 3's "combined" bars, are not invariant to such shifts. This is the well-known identification problem in detailed decompositions (Oaxaca & Ransom, 1999, on the omitted-category problem). The same issue applies to the locale and school-level dummies through the choice of omitted category. (3) Figure 3 has no bar for the constant, even though the constant carries most of the overall gap (about 84%) and more than all of the aesthetics and environment gaps. A reader looking at Figure 3 sees 30% for property taxes without seeing that the twelve covariates together net to about 16%. (4) The location-invariant quantities, the endowments (E) under either reference group, tell a more modest but still meaningful story. Property-tax differences are consistently associated with a positive, significant share of the gap. State aid is consistently associated with a negative share. Donations contribute essentially nothing. The endowment shares for locale also shift a lot across indices (e.g., rural endowment is 65% of the environment gap), which reflects the near-absence of common support: the implied share of White schools in cities is about 3% of the non-White share, and the rural share is about 25 times as high. The non-White coefficients on rural, and the White coefficients on city, are therefore extrapolations. The large offsetting City coefficient and interaction terms (−0.0404 and +0.0391 overall; −0.0786 and +0.0761 environment; Table 2, pp. 9–10) are typical of that situation.

*Timing and interpretation of finance variables.* The paper does not say which fiscal years the comptroller variables cover, or whether they are single-year or averaged. Building conditions in 2015 reflect decades of capital stock, while per-pupil property-tax revenue mostly funds operations and proxies for fiscal capacity. State building aid is paid on approved projects, which ties it mechanically to recent construction. Language like "gaps would be even larger in the absence of state building aid" (p. 2) and "the progressive formula for state building aid is successfully helping to equalize gaps" (p. 11) is counterfactual and causal, and it goes beyond what the authors' own caveat (p. 5) allows. The sensitivity models (p. 11; Appendix Figure A8, Table A13) reportedly show property taxes falling from about 30% to about 20% once taxable property values are added. That is consistent with the property-tax term standing in for community wealth, but the appendix could not be checked. Model 3 also adds community racial composition as a covariate, which is an odd choice when decomposing a racial-composition gap.

*Bottom line.* The descriptive disparities, especially the large gaps in ventilation, humidity, cleanliness, appearance, and access to athletic fields and health offices, are the paper's load-bearing and trustworthy contribution. The decomposition supports a directional statement: differences in local property-tax capacity line up with the gap, and state building aid lines up against it. It does not support the specific percentages, the donations narrative, or the causal policy readings. Proper district-level inference would probably widen the uncertainty around all of these. Parts of the analysis could not be assessed, including all appendix-based robustness checks, the item definitions (Appendix A1), and how the covariates were scaled, and this limits confidence.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's account of the economics-of-education literature on capital spending is compact, current, and mostly accurate. A reader can use it as a reliable map of the quasi-experimental "does capital spending matter" studies. Its positioning on its own question, disparities in realized building conditions, is weaker. The "first comprehensive analysis" claim (p. 1) holds only because of its narrow qualifiers. Several works it cites for other purposes (GAO 1995; NCES 2000; Simons et al. 2010; Sorensen et al. 2024) are closer antecedents than the paper lets on. The sociological, qualitative/legal, environmental-justice and decomposition-methods literatures that bear most on how to read its findings get little or no engagement.

**Strengths:**

- **Citation integrity is clean (checkable).** All 52 reference-list entries (pp. 13–14) are cited in the text or notes, and every in-text citation I found has a reference-list entry. The only slips are typographic: "Kitigawa-Oaxaca-Blinder" (p. 2, Introduction); "LaFortune and Schönholzer (2022)" (p. 2, Literature Review) against "Lafortune" in the references (p. 14); and "Brunner et al (2023)" with the period missing (p. 3).
- **The capital-spending evidence is presented fairly as mixed (checkable).** The paper sorts studies into null effects (Baron 2022; Cellini et al. 2010; Enami et al. 2021; Goncalves 2015; Martorell et al. 2016), delayed or modest effects (Conlin & Thompson 2017; Hong & Zimmer 2016; O'Hagan 2025; Rauscher 2020), and strong positive effects (Biasi et al. 2025; Lafortune & Schönholzer 2022; Neilson & Zimmerman 2014) (p. 2, Literature Review). It does not cherry-pick the positive studies to motivate the topic.
- **The key recent studies are described accurately (knowledge-based, moderate-to-high confidence).** These are Biasi et al. (2025): stacked RD on bond referenda across 29 states, with infrastructure spending raising scores and athletic spending not doing so (p. 3). Lafortune & Schönholzer (2022): Los Angeles, with gains attributed to facility quality and reduced overcrowding (p. 2). Gilraine (2025): air filters in Los Angeles schools after a gas leak, spatial RD (p. 3). Baron (2022): operational referenda raise outcomes and capital referenda do not, which fits its placement among the nulls. Park et al. (2020): heat harms learning and AC mitigates it (p. 3). These match my understanding of those papers.
- **It engages some conflicting evidence on equity (checkable, p. 12, Discussion).** It cites Rauscher & Fiel (2026) as a caution that formulas targeting economic disadvantage may not reduce racial funding gaps as much. That is a useful counterweight to its own "state aid is equalizing" result.
- **The three-domain framing is a real contribution (interpretive).** Aesthetics, environmental conditions, and health/recreational facilities (p. 3) fit the mechanism literature it cites. Treating recreational facilities and health offices as equity outcomes (third gap, p. 3) is a sensible extension beyond the HVAC/air-quality focus of recent economics work.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The novelty claim leans on its qualifiers and undersells the antecedents.** "To our knowledge, the first comprehensive analysis of racial disparities in school building conditions using large-scale building inspection data" (p. 1, Introduction) is defensible only through "inspection data" and "comprehensive." GAO (1995) and NCES (2000) are cited only for "concerns about inadequate funding" (p. 2). From my knowledge (moderate confidence, ~0.65–0.7), both reports broke facility conditions out by school minority enrollment and/or poverty, and both reported worse conditions in high-minority or central-city schools, using administrator surveys rather than inspections. Those reports are direct, if older, antecedents on RQ2.
- **Prior use of the same data source is not flagged.** Sorensen et al. (2024) is described only as "using school-level data from New York State" (p. 3, checkable). The corresponding author co-wrote it, and the reference title (p. 14) shows it studies BCS HVAC conditions. Simons et al. (2010) appears only in the Discussion (p. 12, checkable), as evidence on outcomes. To my knowledge (moderate confidence, ~0.7), it linked an earlier cycle of the New York BCS to absenteeism in upstate schools. A reader should know that this is at least the third study built on BCS data. What is new is the disparity focus, not the data.
- **The finance-disparity gap is framed as more open than it is.** Brunner et al. (2023) is summarized as showing that disadvantaged and minority districts get less facility funding (p. 3). That paper's central finding, as its title signals, is that facility funding depends on property wealth; the reference title (p. 14) is checkable, and my reading of the content is knowledge-based at moderate confidence. The paper's headline decomposition result, property taxes as the largest contributor with state aid partly offsetting (p. 10, Figure 3), therefore confirms the California evidence in a new state and a new outcome more than it newly identifies a mechanism. The Discussion concedes this implicitly (p. 12, "Prior research shows that local revenues play a key role…"). The Introduction's "underlying structural sources" framing (p. 1) does not.
- **A missing bridge undercuts the "much less is known" claim.** The paper says little is known about how funding disparities become condition disparities (p. 3). Martorell et al. (2016) is listed only as a null achievement study (p. 2). Its title, "Capital spending, facility conditions, and student achievement" (checkable, p. 14), signals that it studies how capital spending changes facility conditions, which is the link the paper calls unstudied. My recollection is that it finds bond-funded spending improves facility measures, such as building age, without raising achievement (moderate confidence, ~0.65).
- **Some citations do not support the sentence they are attached to.** Duncombe & Wang (2009) is cited for studies of capital spending's effects on "achievement, attainment, crime, and house prices" (p. 2). To my knowledge (moderate confidence, ~0.7), it is a descriptive survey of state capital-funding programs and capital-outlay distribution, not an outcomes study. Baron et al. (2026) is cited for capital spending producing larger educational benefits in disadvantaged communities (p. 3). Its title concerns "public school funding" and adult crime (p. 13, checkable). My recollection is that it studies operating-funding variation from Michigan's finance reform rather than capital spending (low-to-moderate confidence, ~0.55). The whole heterogeneity sentence (Baron et al.; Biasi et al.; Rauscher 2020) also sits under "disparities in school building conditions remains understudied" (p. 3), but it is about unequal returns to spending, not unequal conditions.
- **Conflicting evidence goes unengaged.** Park et al. (2020) is cited only for heat harming learning (p. 3). To my knowledge (moderate confidence, ~0.7), a central finding of that paper is that Black and Hispanic students are less likely to have school AC and that heat explains part of the racial achievement gap. The paper instead finds mostly non-White New York schools *more* likely to have a satisfactory cooling system, +3.6 pp (p. 7, Table 1). It offers a locale explanation that rests on appendix tables I could not check, and it never notes the tension with the national evidence it cites.
- **Adjacent literatures are thin.**
  - *Sociology of segregation.* Only Derenoncourt et al. (2024) is used (p. 2), a national racial-wealth-gap history. Nothing is cited on district fragmentation, residential segregation, or redlining and school finance.
  - *Qualitative, historical, and legal traditions.* Absent altogether. The obvious omissions are Kozol's *Savage Inequalities* and the Williams v. California facilities litigation.
  - *Environmental justice.* Banzhaf et al. (2019) is the only citation, and it appears only in the Discussion (p. 11).
  - *Decomposition methods.* Only Jann (2008) is cited, in note 9 (p. 13).
- **The "education debt" and environmental-justice framings are asserted, not earned.** Ladson-Billings (2006) and Banzhaf et al. (2019) appear only in the Discussion (pp. 11–12). The claim of "cumulative effects of historically unequal public investments" (p. 12) is not something cross-sectional 2015 data can show, although the paper hedges with "may represent." Banzhaf et al. is also, to my knowledge (moderate-high confidence, ~0.8), known for stressing that disproportionate exposure can come from household sorting and market dynamics as well as from siting decisions. That caveat bears directly on reading school-composition correlations as institutional inequity, and the paper does not draw it.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite this paper for **inspection-based, student-weighted evidence on racial gaps in facility conditions in New York outside NYC in 2015** (pp. 3–8). Include the recreational and health-office measures. For the general fact that high-minority schools report worse facilities, pair or precede it with the older national survey reports (GAO 1995; NCES 2000), after checking those reports' demographic breakouts yourself.
- For the finance mechanism (local property wealth drives facility gaps and state aid partly offsets), treat **Brunner, Schwegman & Vincent (2023)** as the primary antecedent and this paper as corroborating evidence from a different state and a different outcome, not as the originating finding.
- For the "does money for buildings matter" question, **Jackson & Mackevicius (2024)** (cited, p. 2) and **Biasi et al. (2025)** are better one-stop summaries than this paper's list of individual studies. My understanding (moderate confidence) is that the meta-analysis finds positive but lagged average effects of capital spending, a sharper conclusion than "mixed."
- **Verify before repeating:**
  - Baron et al. (2026) as evidence on *capital* spending (p. 3).
  - Duncombe & Wang (2009) as an outcomes study (p. 2).
  - The implication that Alexander & Lewis (2014) documents clear racial differences in reported conditions (p. 1). My recollection (low confidence, ~0.5) is that the 2012–13 FRSS differences by minority enrollment were modest and uneven across building features.
  - O'Hagan (2025) (pp. 2–3), which I cannot assess. Its title ("Inequities and impacts…") suggests it also documents inequities in NYC facility investment. If so, it is a close antecedent that the paper describes only for its attendance effect, and it covers the city this paper excludes (p. 3, note 2).
- **Companion readings (knowledge-based; I am confident these exist, less so on details):**
  - *Environmental justice at schools:* Pastor, Sadd & Morello-Frosch (2002, *Social Science Quarterly*) on air toxics near Los Angeles schools; Mohai et al. (2011, *Health Affairs*) on pollution near Michigan schools and its racial pattern.
  - *Segregation and funding:* Reardon & Owens (2014, *Annual Review of Sociology*); Bischoff (2008, *Urban Affairs Review*) on district fragmentation; Sosina & Weathers (2019, *AERA Open*) on between-district segregation and spending gaps; Lukes & Cleveland (2021, EdWorkingPaper) on redlining and school funding. Cleveland is thanked in the acknowledgments (p. 12).
  - *Facilities-disparity reports:* 21st Century School Fund's *Growth and Disparity* (Filardo et al., 2006), on construction spending by district income and race; GAO's 2020 report on district building-system needs (GAO-20-494).
  - *Qualitative, legal, and teacher-side work:* Kozol's *Savage Inequalities* (1991) and the Williams v. California record, for the tradition that first documented these gaps; Buckley, Schneider & Shang (2004) on facility conditions and teacher retention, one outcome channel the paper does not mention.
- **On the decomposition, read the Oaxaca-Blinder methods literature alongside Figure 3.** Relevant works include Jones (1983, *JHR*) and Oaxaca & Ransom (1999) on the non-identification of detailed "coefficients" contributions, Fortin, Lemieux & Firpo (2011, *Handbook of Labor Economics*), and, for causal interpretation, Jackson & VanderWeele (2018, *Epidemiology*). The paper's per-covariate percentages combine endowment, coefficient and interaction pieces (Figure 3 note, p. 11). That is exactly where this literature warns that attributions depend on normalization and reference-group choices.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Citation mechanics (checkable).* I cross-checked the reference list (pp. 13–14; 52 entries, including the three methods classics and Jann 2008) against the body and notes. Every entry is cited, and no in-text citation lacks an entry. The problems are cosmetic ("Kitigawa," p. 2; "LaFortune," p. 2; "Brunner et al (2023)," p. 3). Several references are 2025–2026 working papers or forthcoming articles whose content I could not verify: O'Hagan 2025; Chung et al. 2025; Rauscher & Fiel 2026; Baron et al. 2026; Backer & Royal 2025; Hailey 2025. The acknowledgments thank O'Hagan (p. 12), whose paper is cited four times; I note that without implying anything improper.

*What the literature review does well.* In under two pages (pp. 2–3), it gives an accurate typology of the capital-spending evidence. It separates spending effects from building-condition effects (Gilraine; Sorensen et al.; Park et al.) and states three gaps. For an *Educational Researcher* Feature article, which must be brief, the econ-of-ed coverage is good. I found no case where a major capital-spending study is placed in the wrong outcome bin. The one partial exception is Martorell et al. (2016), which is correctly binned as null on achievement but whose facility-conditions component is ignored. Cellini et al. (2010) is placed among the nulls. Its main result is house-price capitalization, and I recall its achievement estimates as imprecise rather than cleanly null (low confidence, ~0.5), so that label is common but coarse.

*The novelty claim, precisely.* Readers deciding what to cite this paper for should break the claim into four parts:

1. **Racial disparities in school facilities exist.** Not new. The GAO and NCES survey reports of the 1990s–2000s, the Williams litigation, advocacy reports (Filardo 2021, cited, p. 2, on spending), and a long qualitative tradition all precede it.
2. **Measured with engineer/architect inspection data at scale.** Plausibly new for race-focused analysis. I know of no other peer-reviewed statewide inspection-based disparity study, but my confidence is only moderate: city-level facility condition assessments (Philadelphia and others) have been analyzed in reports and journalism, and Backer & Royal (2025, p. 2) work on Philadelphia buildings. The data themselves are not new to this research team (Sorensen et al. 2024) or to the public-health literature (Simons et al. 2010).
3. **Student-weighted exposure by race, including recreational and health facilities.** Genuinely distinctive, and the paper's most citable descriptive contribution (Figure 2, p. 7; Table 1, p. 6).
4. **Revenue sources explain the gap.** Consistent with, not novel relative to, Brunner et al. (2023), Biasi et al. (2021), and the older capital-finance literature the paper cites (Duncombe & Wang 2009; Sielke 2001). Plummer (2006) is cited only among policy options (p. 12), although it studies how state facility aid changes local tax effort and construction. That question matters for whether New York's building aid really "equalizes" or partly substitutes for local effort.

*Conflicting evidence and how it changes interpretation.* Two bodies of evidence cut against simple readings of the results and are not engaged.

First, cooling. The paper's own Table 1 shows mostly non-White schools slightly *ahead* on satisfactory cooling (p. 7). Park et al. (2020), which the paper cites, is known for the opposite national pattern (my knowledge, moderate confidence). A reader should take the New York result as context-specific (upstate rural White schools with window units; note 10, p. 13) rather than as evidence against national AC disparities.

Second, the design of state building aid. The paper reads the negative contribution of state building aid (−17%, p. 10, Figure 3) as evidence that New York's "progressive formula … is successfully helping to equalize gaps" (p. 11). The school-finance literature on reimbursement-style capital aid (Duncombe & Wang 2009 and Sielke 2001, both cited, discuss program types) makes a relevant point. My understanding (moderate confidence) is that aid of this kind flows only to districts that initiate and locally approve projects, so aid receipt is partly an outcome of local capacity and of recent investment. That literature supports a more cautious reading than "successfully helping to equalize." The paper's own caveat about reverse causality (p. 5) points the same way, but the literature it cites is not brought to bear on this specific inference.

*The decomposition literature and Figure 3.* Only Jann (2008) is cited for implementation (note 9, p. 13). I summed the component rows of Table 2 (pp. 9–10); this is my arithmetic, checkable against the table.

- The per-covariate totals reproduce Figure 3. For property taxes: 0.0425 endowments + 0.0151 coefficients − 0.0328 interactions = 0.0248, about 30% of the 0.0830 gap. For state aid: −0.0107 + 0.0118 − 0.0153 = −0.0142, about −17%.
- The listed coefficient rows for the overall index sum to about −0.010, while the reported coefficients total is 0.0603 (p. 9). The unreported intercept therefore carries about 0.070, roughly 84% of the gap.
- All the covariate bars in Figure 3 together account for only about 16% of the gap.

The decomposition literature is the right place to read about this. It covers why detailed coefficient contributions and the constant are not identified independently of normalization (Jones 1983; Oaxaca & Ransom 1999; Fortin, Lemieux & Firpo 2011), and why "largest contributor" language needs care when most of the gap is unexplained. That literature changes how the headline "property taxes explain the largest share" (p. 1, Introduction; p. 10) should be read. Property taxes are the largest *identified* contributor to a gap that is mostly unexplained by the model.

*Placement in adjacent fields.* The paper sits squarely in economics of education and school finance. Public health appears through Simons et al. (2010) and Michael et al. (2015), but only as outcome evidence. The sociology of segregation is represented by one national wealth-gap paper (Derenoncourt et al. 2024, p. 2), while the more directly relevant work on district fragmentation, redlining, and between-district funding gaps is absent. Qualitative and legal traditions are absent. Environmental justice appears once in the Discussion. For an *Educational Researcher* audience, the "education debt" framing (Ladson-Billings 2006, p. 12) is a natural hook. Earning it would take historical or longitudinal evidence, or engagement with the segregation-and-finance literature, and the paper offers neither. It works as a rhetorical frame, not a finding.

*Confidence note.* My checkable assessments (citation integrity, what the paper says about each citation and where, Table 2 arithmetic) are high confidence. My knowledge-based claims about what the cited and omitted works contain carry the individual confidence labels given above. I am least sure about the details of the 2025–2026 working papers and about the demographic breakouts in the 1995/2000 federal reports, which readers should verify directly. The online supplement (Appendix Tables A1–A13, Figures A1–A8) was not available, so I could not check any claim that rests on it, including the locale explanation for the cooling result and the Model 3 sensitivity result (p. 11).

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a short, well-organized descriptive paper. Most of the numbers in the text match the exhibits: nearly every percentage-point gap and significance statement in the Results matches Table 1, the Figure 2 SD values match the prose exactly, and the Figure 3 shares can be recovered from Table 2. The paper does have one outright text–figure swap and two significance markers in Table 1 that its own means and cell sizes cannot support. The bigger problem is interpretive. The prose describing the decomposition, and the abstract, claim more than Table 2 and Figure 3 show. In particular, a component that is mostly an unreported intercept difference is read as evidence about funding channels, and a descriptive decomposition is described in causal terms.

**Strengths:**

- The structure is clean and easy to follow. There are three research questions (p. 1), and each maps onto one block of results: Figure 1 answers RQ1, Table 1 and Figure 2 answer RQ2, and Table 2 and Figure 3 answer RQ3. The paper is 14 pages, and a reader can locate the load-bearing material quickly.
- Most of the Table 1 prose is accurate (checkable). Of the 17 percentage-point gaps quoted on pp. 6–7, all match Table 1 column (3 – 1) (p. 6) to the decimal. Every significance label the text gives (e.g., vermin "p < .1", cooling satisfactory "p < .05", heating "p < .1", gymnasium "p < .1", swimming pool "p < .01") matches the asterisk printed in Table 1.
- The Figure 2 prose (pp. 7–8) reproduces all 24 cell values in the rendered heat map (p. 7) exactly (checkable).
- Figure 3 (p. 11) can be reproduced from Table 2 (pp. 9–10). Summing the endowment, coefficient, and interaction rows for each covariate and dividing by the 0.0830 gap gives property taxes 29.9%, donations 6.7%, and state building aid –17.1%, which are the 30%, 7%, and –17% quoted on p. 10 (checkable).
- The text states the limits of the decomposition plainly: it "remains descriptive" and "does not establish causal relationships" (p. 5).
- The Discussion closes with a limitations paragraph (p. 12) that names the cross-sectional design, the subjective items, and the descriptive nature of the analysis.

**Weaknesses:**

- **Text–figure swap on p. 5 (checkable).** The text says "Eighty-five percent have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating." Rendered Figure 1a (p. 5) shows Appearance good = 0.85 and Lighting quality good = 0.75. The school-weighted means from Table 1 (p. 6) confirm that the figure is correct (appearance ≈ 0.852, lighting ≈ 0.752), so the text has the two reversed.
- **Two Table 1 asterisks the table's own means and Ns cannot support (checkable, derived).** Swimming pool is –0.033** (p. 6). With 0.152 vs 0.119 and n = 940 vs 519, an approximate two-sample test gives t ≈ 1.8 (p ≈ .07), which would earn at most "+". Stadium condition satisfactory is –0.224*, but the same calculation gives t ≈ 9.9, which should be "**". The text repeats the pool result as "(p < .01)" (p. 7). The pattern looks like a transposition or typo, but I cannot confirm that without the data.
- **Table 2 does not show the intercept (checkable, and it drives the interpretation).** In the overall column, the detailed endowment rows sum to 0.0338 (the summary says 0.0337) and the interaction rows sum to –0.0110 (summary: –0.0110). The detailed coefficient rows, however, sum to about –0.0095, against a summary coefficients component of 0.0603 (pp. 9–10). The unreported difference of about 0.070, which is 84% of the gap, is the difference in constants. It is about 0.093 for aesthetics, about 0.091 for environmental conditions, and about 0.026 for health/recreation. So when the text says the coefficients component "is most substantial, suggesting that contributing factors (e.g., school characteristics and school funding) have different associations … in ways that exacerbate inequality" (p. 8), it is attributing to the covariates a quantity that comes mainly from the intercept. Across the covariates themselves, the coefficient differences net to about zero or slightly negative.
- **Figure 3 has no "unexplained" bar (checkable, derived).** Summed over all 12 covariates, the per-covariate shares come to about 16% of the overall gap. Figure 3 (p. 11) gives no bar for the remaining ~84%. A reader who sees "property taxes explain 30%" can easily assume the displayed bars add up to the whole gap.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: a reporting omission, not an error in the paper.*

- **"Explained by property taxes" is a composite (interpretive, grounded in Table 2).** The 30% figure adds the endowment (0.0425), coefficient (0.0151), and interaction (–0.0328) pieces (p. 10, Table 2). Taken alone, the endowment piece, which is the "differences in property taxes" the text describes, is about 51% of the gap. The interaction piece largely offsets it. The prose describes the composite as "differences in local property taxes" (p. 2, p. 10).
- **Causal wording contradicts the p. 5 caveat (interpretive).** The abstract says state aid "helps reduce these disparities." Page 11 says the formula "is successfully helping to equalize gaps." Page 12 says donations "contribute meaningfully." For the donations point, note that the donations endowment term is 0.0020 and not significant (p. 9, Table 2).
- **Abstract overstatement (checkable).** The abstract lists gymnasiums among outcomes where schools serving more students of color are "significantly more likely" to have reduced access. The gymnasium gap is –0.025 with the p < .1 marker (p. 6, Table 1), which the text itself calls marginal (p. 7).
- **Abstract omissions (checkable).** The abstract does not say that New York City is excluded, even though the title and abstract say "New York State" (the exclusion is disclosed on p. 3 and in note 2). It does not give the 2015 data year, and it does not say that most of the decomposed gap is not accounted for by the listed factors.
- **Group definition drift (checkable).** The introduction (p. 2) describes "Schools serving predominantly Black and Hispanic students." The comparison group in Table 1 is actually ">50% non-White", which also includes Asian, Native American, and multiracial students (p. 6).
- **Condition gaps may be presence gaps (derived, partly inferential).** The "condition satisfactory" items appear to be unconditional shares: stadium 0.32 with 0.29 satisfactory, and athletic fields 0.88 with 0.80 satisfactory (Figure 1c, p. 5). If so, the satisfactory share conditional on having the facility is nearly identical by group. For stadiums it is 0.386/0.428 ≈ 0.90 (White) vs 0.162/0.181 ≈ 0.90 (non-White). For athletic fields it is 0.889 vs 0.913, higher in non-White schools (Table 1, p. 6). The claims that these facilities "are in worse condition on average" (p. 2) and "in significantly better condition in predominantly White schools" (p. 7) may therefore restate the presence gap rather than reflect condition. I could not check the item definitions (Appendix Table A1).
- **Sample sizes do not reconcile (checkable).** The text reports 2,352 schools with full coverage (p. 4), and the school-level breakdown 1,409 + 369 + 436 + 138 = 2,352 agrees. But Table 1 reports 940 + 912 + 519 = 2,371 (p. 6). Table 2 has N = 1,440 (p. 10), while the two groups it compares total 940 + 519 = 1,459 in Table 1. Both discrepancies are exactly 19 schools, and neither is explained. Note 4 calls the 2,473 BCS schools "the analytic sample" (p. 13), which is a third meaning of that phrase.
- **Figure 2 significance claims cannot be checked from the paper (checkable absence).** The heat map (p. 7) shows no significance markers. The text on p. 8 uses a nonstandard threshold ("0.01 SD (p < .005)"), a malformed phrase ("99% significance level"), and p-values attached to near-zero values ("0.00 SD (p < .05)", "–0.03 SD (p < .01)"). These are easy to misread as tests against the mean rather than against the most advantaged group.
- **Typos and naming inconsistencies (checkable).** "Kitigawa" (p. 2) vs "Kitagawa" (p. 2 citation, p. 4, references). "LaFortune" (p. 2) vs "Lafortune" (p. 1, p. 12, references). "Brunner et al (2023)" lacks a period (p. 3). "(–17 %)" has a stray space (p. 10). "Title 1" appears where "Title I" is meant (p. 11). "Model 2" is introduced on p. 11 without Table 2 ever being labeled as Model 2. The Discussion lists "type" among the controls (p. 12), but it is not among the covariates listed on pp. 4–5.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Table 1 (p. 6) and its prose on pp. 6–7 closely. These are the paper's most reliable exhibit and narrative. Before citing the swimming-pool result as significant, or the stadium-condition result as only p < .05, check the asterisks against the means and Ns.
- Do not quote the p. 5 figures for lighting and appearance from the text. Use Figure 1a: appearance 85%, lighting 75%.
- Treat the intro's "25 percentage points less likely to have satisfactory ventilation" (p. 2) as 26 (25.9 in Table 1).
- When citing "property taxes explain 30%" (p. 10) or "nearly one-third" (p. 12), be aware of two things. The figure combines endowment, coefficient, and interaction terms. And the covariates in Figure 3 jointly account for only about 16% of the overall gap, with the rest in an intercept difference that neither Table 2 nor Figure 3 shows.
- Discount the p. 8 reading of the "coefficients component" as evidence about funding associations. Most of it is the omitted constant.
- Read the state-aid and donations conclusions (abstract; pp. 11–12) as descriptive associations, which is how the paper itself frames them on p. 5.
- For Figure 2, the p. 8 significance statements are tests against the best-off group for each index, not against zero or the mean. They cannot be checked from the figure, and Appendix Table A7 was not available.
- The poverty and locale sections (p. 8), the Model 1/3 sensitivity check (p. 11: "roughly 30% to roughly 20%"), and the latent-factor robustness check (note 11) rely entirely on the online appendix. A time-constrained reader can skim them but should not cite them without the supplement.
- Remember throughout that "New York State" here means New York State excluding New York City (p. 3, note 2), using 2015 inspection data.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization.* The paper follows a standard structure: introduction with three RQs, literature review, data, method, results, discussion. It is economical, and each RQ has one or two exhibits. The load-bearing exhibits are Table 1 (the school-composition gaps) and Table 2 with Figure 3 (the decomposition). Figure 1 is context, and Figure 2 is the student-weighted version of RQ2. Several claims in the prose are delegated wholly to the supplement: the poverty and locale comparisons (Appendix Tables A5, A6, A8–A10 and Figure A4), the per-index shares (Figures A5–A7), the Model 1/3 sensitivity check (Figure A8, Table A13), and the SEM check (Tables A11–A12). None of these could be checked here. The Method section describes the tests (t tests; a cluster bootstrap with 200 replications, cluster level not stated; "robust" SEs in Table 2) but does not say whether the district-level finance variables were accounted for when computing standard errors. That point belongs more to the methods dimension, but readers should note it.

*Exhibit self-containment.* Table 1's note does not define the White-share thresholds; they appear only in the text (p. 6). Table 2's note does not name the omitted categories (elementary school, and presumably suburban locale) and has no constant row. The sign convention also flips between exhibits. Table 1 reports (non-White – White), so the gaps are negative. Table 2 reports (White – non-White), so the gaps are positive. Figure 1 has no note, no sample size, and an unlabeled y-axis. The Figure 2 legend bins share endpoints (e.g., "−0.02 to 0.03" and "0.03 to 0.08"), and the text says the SD values are on the "x-axis" (p. 7) when the x-axis actually lists the four indices. The index means in Table 2's summary panel differ slightly from the Table 1 averages: health/recreation is 0.6532 vs 0.648 (White) and 0.5529 vs 0.549 (non-White). That is consistent with the 1,440 vs 1,459 sample difference, but the paper does not flag it. The p. 8 statement that "the standard deviations of these indices range from 0.14 to 0.17" does not appear in any main-text table.

*Fidelity of the decomposition narrative.* This is the most consequential exposition issue. The overall gap is 0.0830. Table 2 splits it into E = 0.0337, C = 0.0603, and I = –0.0110. The endowment and interaction detail rows sum to their totals, but the coefficient detail rows sum to about –0.0095, so about 0.070 of the "coefficients" component is the constant. That is standard Oaxaca output. The problem is that the paper never mentions it, and then interprets the coefficients component as covariates having "different associations … in ways that exacerbate inequality" (p. 8). Figure 3 compounds this by showing only covariate bars, which net to about 16% of the gap. The per-covariate percentages are arithmetically correct. What a reader lacks is the denominator logic: what the bars leave out, and that each bar mixes three components with different meanings. The p. 8 claim that the coefficients component is the largest "for most indices" is conservative: it is the largest for all four (C > E in every column, p. 9).

*Figure 2 and student-group results.* The introduction's "0.32 SD below" (Hispanic), "0.19 SD below" (Black), and "ranging from 0.05 SD to 0.21 SD above the mean" (Asian 0.05, multiracial 0.10, AIAN 0.15, White 0.21) all match the Overall column of rendered Figure 2 (p. 7). The p. 8 description says Hispanic students experience "the worst school building conditions" and gives their recreation index as –0.16. On recreation and health, however, Black students (–0.19) are worse than Hispanic students (–0.16) (Figure 2). The number is quoted correctly, but the "worst" framing covers only three of the four indices.

*Compact text-vs-exhibit audit.*

The Adequate rating (rather than Strong) reflects four problems a careful reader could be misled by: the p. 5 swap, the two implausible Table 1 asterisks, the unexplained sample counts, and above all a decomposition narrative (p. 8, Figure 3, abstract) that does not tell readers most of the gap sits in an unreported constant. None of these makes the headline descriptive disparities unreliable. The table-derived t-statistics are approximations that assume independent two-sample proportions using the Table 1 Ns. Missing data on individual items could change them somewhat, but not enough to produce p < .01 for the pool difference.
