### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper documents, with item-level building-inspection data for about 2,350 New York public schools outside New York City, that schools serving mostly students of color have measurably worse realized building conditions than mostly White schools. The gaps are largest for ventilation, humidity, mold, cleanliness, athletic fields/stadiums, and health offices. Weighting by students, Hispanic and Black students attend the worst-condition buildings. That descriptive contribution is genuine, well organized, and useful for a broad-audience Feature Article. The paper's most quotable claims come from a Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder (KOB) decomposition: property taxes are "the largest contributor," state building aid is "successfully helping to equalize," and donations "contribute meaningfully." Those claims are considerably stronger than a descriptive decomposition using district-level finance flows can support, and they should not be what the paper is mainly cited for.

**Strengths:**

- **[Checkable]** Outcome measures come from inspections, not funding. The paper measures realized conditions from the 2015 Building Condition Survey (BCS), which the paper describes as conducted by a team that includes a licensed architecture/engineering firm (p. 3). It organizes 24 items into three domains (p. 8). This answers the paper's stated gap: prior disparity work measures funding or capital outlay (Brunner et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2022; pp. 1, 3). **[Interpretive]** Moving from dollars to conditions is the paper's most distinctive and durable contribution.
- **[Checkable]** The item-level gaps are large and specific, not just index-level. Mostly non-White minus mostly White: ventilation satisfactory −0.259, humidity −0.200, no mold −0.071, cleanliness −0.146, athletic fields −0.194, external stadium −0.247, health office −0.115, all p < .01 (p. 6, Table 1). Detail at this level can inform policy on HVAC and health offices in a way a single spending gap cannot.
- **[Checkable]** The student-weighted exposure analysis (p. 7, Figure 2; pp. 7–8) partly unbundles the pooled "non-White" category. On the overall index, Hispanic students are at −0.32 SD, Black students at −0.19 SD, Asian at +0.05, multiracial at +0.10, American Indian or Alaska Native (AIAN) at +0.15, and White at +0.21. **[Interpretive]** This is a distinct contribution. It shows the disadvantage falls on Hispanic and Black students specifically, not on "students of color" uniformly, and readers should lean on it more than on the three-category school typology.
- **[Checkable]** The property-tax association is consistent across indices. Summing its endowment, coefficient, and interaction rows in Table 2 gives about 30% of the gap for every index: overall 0.0248/0.0830; aesthetics 0.0267/0.0885; environmental 0.0173/0.0602; health/recreation 0.0303/0.1002 (my arithmetic from pp. 9–10, Table 2). The paper reports it attenuates to about 20% when community covariates, including taxable property values, are added (p. 11; Appendix Table A13 / Figure A8 could not be checked).
- **[Checkable]** The paper includes health offices and recreational facilities (pp. 3, 5), which it argues are understudied (p. 3). **[Interpretive]** This widens what counts as "facilities equity."
- **[Interpretive]** The paper itself shows why its recommendation to report facility conditions systematically (p. 12) matters. Statewide census-style inspection ended after the 2015 cycle, replaced by roughly 500–560 schools a year (p. 3, note 3).

**Weaknesses:**

- **[Checkable]** Table 2 and Figure 3 do not show the unexplained intercept. The covariate-level rows in Table 2 reproduce the endowment (0.0337) and interaction (−0.0110) totals exactly. But the coefficient rows sum to about −0.0095 against a coefficient total of 0.0603 (overall index, pp. 9–10, Table 2; my arithmetic). That implies about 0.070, roughly 84% of the 0.083 gap, sits in the group intercept difference, which neither Table 2 nor Figure 3 (p. 11) reports. The Figure 3 bars net to only about 16% of the gap. **[Interpretive]** "Property taxes are the largest contributor" is true among the listed covariates. But a reader of the abstract would reasonably infer that finance variables explain most of the gap, and on this accounting they do not.
- **[Checkable]** The state-aid claim rests on components that are mostly not significant. The −17% overall figure (p. 10 text; p. 11, Figure 3) combines an endowment of −0.0107 (p < .05), a coefficient of +0.0118 (n.s.), and an interaction of −0.0153 (n.s.) (pp. 9–10, Table 2). No standard error is reported for the combined share. For the health/recreation index the same three rows sum to +0.0057, meaning state aid slightly *widens* that gap. So "compensatory" does not hold across all four indices.
- **[Interpretive]** Causal wording outruns the stated design. The Methods (p. 5) and Limitations (p. 12) say the decomposition is descriptive and non-causal. Yet the abstract says aid "helps reduce these disparities" (p. 1), the introduction says aid "meaningfully narrows infrastructure gaps" (p. 2), and the Results say the formula "is successfully helping to equalize gaps" (p. 11). These are counterfactual, causal claims. There is also a specific reverse-causality issue the paper does not discuss **(reviewer knowledge, not from the paper)**: New York building aid reimburses approved capital projects, so districts that recently renovated mechanically receive more aid per pupil *and* have better-rated buildings.
- **[Checkable]** The donations claim is a slope difference, not a levels difference. The 7% share (p. 10) comes mainly from the coefficient component (0.0056, p < .01). The endowment component, which is the levels difference behind the paper's story that "White communities may use their access to wealth to donate," is 0.0020 and not significant (pp. 9–10, Table 2). "Contribute meaningfully" (p. 12) overstates this.
- **[Checkable]** There is a mismatch in timing and level between the outcome and the explanatory variables. Building conditions are a stock built up over decades, while the finance variables are district-level per-pupil amounts (p. 4; Table 2 note, p. 10). The main text does not say which fiscal year(s) they cover. Table 2 reports "robust" standard errors (p. 10 note), with no mention of clustering by district, even though schools in the same district share identical finance values.
- **[Checkable]** Some claims are worded more broadly than the analysis. The introduction describes "schools serving predominantly Black and Hispanic students" (p. 2), but the category is >50% non-White of any group, including Asian and multiracial students (pp. 4, 6). The abstract lists gymnasiums among "significantly" worse outcomes (p. 1), but the gymnasium gap is −0.025, p < .1 (p. 6, Table 1). The title says "New York State" while New York City is excluded (note 2, p. 13).
- **[Checkable, minor]** Sample counts do not reconcile. Table 1's group sizes sum to 2,371 (940 + 912 + 519; p. 6) against a stated linked sample of 2,352 (p. 4). The KOB sample is 1,440 (p. 10, Table 2), whereas 940 + 519 = 1,459. Neither difference is explained.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for:** the existence and approximate size of racial gaps in *realized*, inspection-rated building conditions in New York outside NYC as of 2015, especially ventilation, humidity, mold, athletic facilities, and health offices (p. 6, Table 1).
- **Cite it for:** student-weighted evidence that Hispanic students, then Black students, attend the worst-condition buildings, while Asian, multiracial, and AIAN students do not (p. 7, Figure 2).
- **Cite it for:** a descriptive association. Differences in district per-pupil property-tax revenue line up with about 30% of the between-group gap across all four indices, and about 20% with community covariates added (pp. 9–11). This is consistent with, but not proof of, a local-wealth channel.
- **Do not cite it for:** "local property taxes are the largest driver/cause" of the gap. The analysis is descriptive, and most of the gap (about 84% by my arithmetic from Table 2) is left in an unreported intercept term.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: a reporting omission, not an error in the paper.*

- **Do not cite it for:** "state building aid reduces/equalizes racial gaps." The design cannot support that counterfactual. Aid is plausibly endogenous to recent construction, only the endowment piece is significant, and the sign flips for the health/recreation index.
- **Do not cite it for:** "private donations drive racial facility gaps." The levels difference in donations is small and not significant (Table 2).
- **Do not cite it for:** current conditions or New York State as a whole. The data are one 2015 cross-section and exclude NYC (p. 3; note 2). **(Reviewer knowledge)** NYC enrolls a large share of the state's Black and Hispanic students, and facility-related spending since 2015 (e.g., pandemic-era federal funds) may have changed HVAC conditions.
- **Open questions:** Do these gaps persist in post-2015 data? What do they look like in NYC? Do the finance associations survive district-clustered inference and explicit handling of the fiscally dependent large-city districts? **(Reviewer knowledge, unverified against the paper: Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, and Yonkers do not levy their own school property taxes, and the paper does not say how their property-tax variable is measured.)** Does variation in the building-aid formula causally change conditions?

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Novelty.* The paper's "to our knowledge, the first comprehensive analysis of racial disparities in school building conditions using large-scale building inspection data" (p. 1) is hedged, and within its scope it is plausible. The novelty is the question and the linkage, not the data source. The same New York BCS underlies Sorensen et al. (2024) on HVAC effects (p. 3), and Simons et al. (2010), cited on p. 12, studies building conditions and absenteeism in upstate New York (I did not verify that paper's data source). **[Interpretive, reviewer knowledge]** Other states and large districts run facility-condition assessments, so "first" should be read as "first in this form," not "first evidence that conditions differ by race." Nationally, NCES's survey-based report (Alexander & Lewis, 2014, cited p. 1) already found worse reported conditions in schools serving more students of color. What is genuinely new is inspection-based item detail at near-census scale for one state, linked to demographics and finance. The "realized conditions rather than funding" framing (pp. 1, 12) is apt and is the paper's clearest conceptual contribution. A real, underappreciated gap separates dollars spent from the air quality and facilities students actually have.

*Significance and how the decomposition should be read.* The descriptive findings matter. The ventilation and humidity gaps of 20–26 percentage points (p. 6, Table 1) fall on exactly the dimensions the paper's own literature review links to learning (Sorensen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2020; p. 3). The explanatory half is weaker than its prominence suggests. The abstract gives equal billing to the descriptive gaps and to the KOB-based finance claims, and the finance claims are what policy audiences will quote. Three features of Table 2 limit what they can bear. First, the listed covariates jointly account for only a small net share of the gap. Most of it is in the intercept, which is not shown, so "largest contributor" is a ranking within a minority share. Second, the combined E+C+I shares in Figure 3 mix a well-defined endowment component with coefficient and interaction components that are imprecise and, for continuous variables, depend on the reference point. Only the endowment rows give a clean "levels differ" story. On those rows, property taxes (0.0425, p < .01) and state aid (−0.0107, p < .05) hold up, and donations (0.0020, n.s.) do not. Third, the explanatory variables are current district finance flows, used to explain a building stock that reflects decades of investment. Property-tax revenue proxies local fiscal capacity reasonably well; the paper's Model 3 attenuation with taxable property values (p. 11) supports that reading. But it also funds operating costs and debt service, so it is not a specific capital channel. State building aid is the most problematic variable. Because aid follows approved projects **(reviewer knowledge)**, a positive aid–condition association is what one would expect even if the formula did nothing to equalize. The paper's "successfully helping to equalize" (p. 11) therefore overreaches. The finding is compatible with that conclusion but cannot establish it.

*Generalizability.* The boundaries are drawn partly honestly. NYC's exclusion is disclosed and justified (note 2), and the single 2015 cycle is disclosed (p. 3). The consequences go unstated: the "mostly non-White" group outside NYC is a particular mix of small-city and suburban schools, and the title and Discussion speak of "New York" generally (pp. 1, 11). The three-category typology (>80% White / 50–80% / >50% non-White; p. 4) is coarse. It groups predominantly Asian suburban schools with high-poverty urban Hispanic and Black schools, which Figure 2 suggests have very different conditions. Note 7 acknowledges the coarseness. Because the data are from 2015, the paper cannot speak to present conditions, and statewide inspection data comparable to 2015 no longer exist (note 3). The fiscal and institutional levers the paper discusses, including New York's wealth-equalized building aid and local bond financing, are specific enough to New York that the finance findings may travel less well than the descriptive gaps. States with more centralized capital finance could look quite different.

*Standing and follow-on work.* For the descriptive question in its setting, this is likely the best available evidence. It is more granular and more objective than survey-based national reports, and it is the natural reference for "racial gaps in inspected building conditions." It is not the best evidence on *why* the gaps exist or on whether state aid closes them. Quasi-experimental capital-finance studies cited in the paper (e.g., Biasi et al., 2025; Brunner et al., 2023) remain the reference points for funding mechanisms. The paper sets up several obvious extensions: exploiting variation in the building-aid formula or referendum outcomes to test the equalization claim causally; linking condition gaps to student outcomes by race (the authors propose this, p. 12); using the post-2015 annual inspection samples to track change; extending to NYC; and replacing the three-category typology with continuous composition or student-level exposure throughout. Its policy recommendations are sensible but generic: expand progressive aid, reduce reliance on local wealth, improve transparency (p. 12). The transparency recommendation is the one its own evidence supports most directly.

*Calibration.* As a short ER Feature Article aimed at a broad audience, the paper does what the format rewards. It establishes a clearly important descriptive fact with new, more objective data and presents it accessibly, and that alone makes it a worthwhile contribution. It falls short of "strong" because the headline explanatory and policy claims in the abstract and Discussion are stated more causally and more confidently than a descriptive decomposition with an unreported intercept and endogenous aid measures can bear, and readers are likely to cite those claims first. It is not "weak," because the core descriptive contribution is clear, credible on its face, and not oversold.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

The paper names its data sources, writes out the threefold decomposition, and reports the full detailed decomposition with standard errors. Its main exhibits also hold together: Table 1's index rows follow from its item rows, Figure 1 matches the pooled Table 1 means, and Figure 3 can be rebuilt exactly from Table 2. Independent reproduction is a different matter. The article has no data availability statement, no code or replication package, no software version, and no documented way to obtain the core dataset (the 2015 Building Condition Survey, which the Acknowledgements say NYSED supplied directly). The sample counts do not reconcile across the text and tables, and several construction steps a replicator would need are left out: fiscal years, building-to-school aggregation, reference categories, and the bootstrap cluster. Readers can check the paper's internal arithmetic but cannot re-derive the headline decomposition from what the article reports.

Labels used below: **[Checkable]** marks a fact about what the paper states or reports, which an overseer can verify against the PDF. **[Judgment]** marks my interpretation, including what I know about whether the data are available outside the paper.

**Strengths:**

- **[Checkable]** The decomposition is written out algebraically (p. 4). The endowments term is weighted by β_NW, the coefficients term is evaluated at X_NW, and an interaction term is included. That answers the question of whose coefficients serve as the reference. The software is named: Jann's (2008) `oaxaca` in Stata (p. 13, note 9). The SE type is stated as "Robust standard errors" (p. 10, Table 2 note).
- **[Checkable]** Table 2 (pp. 9–10) reports all 12 covariates' endowment, coefficient, and interaction contributions, with SEs, for all four indices, along with group means and N = 1,440. The summary rows add up: E + C + I equals the gap in all four columns (for example, 0.0337 + 0.0603 − 0.0110 = 0.0830 for the overall index). The detailed endowment and interaction rows sum to their summary rows within 0.0001.
- **[Checkable]** Figure 3 (p. 11) can be regenerated from Table 2. For the overall index, adding each covariate's E + C + I and dividing by 0.0830 gives property taxes +29.9%, state building aid −17.1%, and donations +6.7%. These match the text (p. 10: "30%", "–17 %", "7%") and the bar lengths.
- **[Checkable]** The indices are transparently built. Averaging the 6 aesthetics items, 9 environmental items, and 9 health/recreation items in Table 1 (p. 6) reproduces the "average" rows exactly in all three columns (e.g., 0.897/0.850/0.648 for mostly White schools). The item count matches the "24 building condition measures" on p. 8. The overall index in Table 2 is the mean of the three sub-indices: (0.8977 + 0.8507 + 0.6532)/3 = 0.8005.
- **[Checkable]** Figure 1 (p. 5) matches the enrollment-weighted pooled Table 1 means to two decimals on every item (e.g., overall satisfactory 0.84, ventilation 0.67, stadium 0.32). So the descriptive exhibits appear to come from one consistent file.
- **[Checkable]** Three data inputs carry enough identifying detail to locate: NCES CCD, Urban Institute MEPS (cited to Gutierrez et al., 2022), and ACS EdTab 2013–2017 (p. 4). **[Judgment]** CCD, MEPS, and the NCES EDGE ACS-ED tabulations are publicly downloadable (high confidence). The NYS Comptroller's school-district financial data are also publicly posted (moderately high confidence).

**Weaknesses:**

- **[Checkable]** No data availability statement, replication package, repository link, or "available on request" line appears anywhere in the back matter (pp. 12–13: Acknowledgements, ORCID iDs, Funding, Declaration of Conflicting Interests, Supplemental Material "available online"). The only statement about how the core data were obtained is that NYSED's Office of Facilities Planning "provid[ed] data and assist[ed] in data interpretation" (p. 12). **[Judgment]** I do not know of a public school-level release of the 2015 BCS microdata. A replicator would probably have to request it from NYSED, and the paper gives no request pathway (low-to-moderate confidence on availability).
- **[Checkable]** The sample counts do not reconcile. The text chain is 2,926 → 2,875 (minus 51 charters; p. 13, note 4) → 2,473 "cleaned" BCS schools (p. 3) → 2,352 merged schools "with full coverage of variables" (p. 4; 1,409 + 369 + 436 + 138 = 2,352 does check). But Table 1's group Ns sum to 940 + 912 + 519 = 2,371 (p. 6), which is 19 more than the stated analytic sample. The decomposition uses N = 1,440 (p. 10), while Table 1's mostly White plus mostly non-White schools number 940 + 519 = 1,459, which is 19 more. **[Judgment]** One plausible explanation is 19 schools lacking decomposition covariates, but the paper does not say so. The 121 schools lost between 2,473 and 2,352 are also unexplained. Note 6 excludes BOCES institutions but gives no count.
- **[Checkable]** Several steps a replicator would have to guess are not described:
  - what "cleaned" involved for the BCS (p. 3), including how building-level inspections were aggregated to schools, even though p. 3 says the survey covers "all occupied public school buildings";
  - the fiscal year(s) of the Comptroller variables, and whether they are single-year or averaged;
  - the CCD and MEPS data years;
  - the per-pupil denominator for "pp = thousands of dollars per pupil" (p. 10, Table 2 note), and whether district totals are assigned to every school in a district;
  - which Comptroller revenue lines define "donations," "bond revenues," and "federal building aid" (p. 4);
  - the units of enrollment;
  - how "Stadium condition satisfactory" and similar items are coded for schools that lack the facility. **[Judgment]** The Table 1 values (0.386 vs. 0.428 for stadiums, p. 6) imply such schools were coded 0, but this is not stated.
- **[Checkable]** Reference categories for the dummy sets are never stated. The Table 2 rows (Middle/High/Other grades; City/Town/Rural) imply that elementary and suburb are omitted, but that is an inference. The intercept's contribution to the coefficients component is not reported. The detailed coefficient rows for the overall index sum to −0.0095, against a reported coefficients total of 0.0603 (pp. 9–10). That leaves an implied, unreported constant term of about 0.070, roughly 84% of the gap. The same pattern holds in the other columns (implied constant about 0.093, 0.091, and 0.026). No `oaxaca` options are reported (e.g., `normalize()` for categorical variables, weighting). **[Judgment]** Without normalization, the per-variable coefficient and interaction contributions for the dummy sets depend on the omitted category. Figure 3's "combined" percentages include those terms (p. 11, Figure 3 note), so they are not fully pinned down by the text.
- **[Checkable]** The student-weighted exposure analysis says it uses "a nonparametric cluster bootstrap with resampling (200 replications)" (p. 4). It gives neither the clustering unit nor a random seed. Figure 2 (p. 7) reports point estimates only. Significance appears only in the prose (p. 8), which includes irregular thresholds such as "p < .005" and a "99% significance level." Full results are in Appendix Table A7, which I could not check.
- **[Checkable]** Table 2 uses robust (not clustered) SEs (p. 10), although every fiscal regressor comes from district-level Comptroller data (p. 4). **[Judgment]** Schools in the same district share identical fiscal values, so the reported SEs probably overstate precision for the finance contributions. This is stated, so it is reproducible, but a replicator should expect clustered SEs to be larger.
- **[Checkable]** Two significance marks in Table 1 cannot be reproduced from the reported proportions and group Ns. I recomputed them as two-sample tests of proportions with N = 940 vs. 519.
  - Swimming pool, −0.033**: z ≈ 1.8, p ≈ .07, which would earn "+" rather than "**". The text repeats "p < .01" (p. 7).
  - Stadium condition satisfactory, −0.224*: z ≈ 9.9, which would earn "**".
  - The other 22 items' marks are consistent with this calculation, with heating (z ≈ 1.6, marked +) at the border.
  - **[Judgment]** These look like swapped stars, but item-level missingness or a different test could matter. The paper does not say which t test was used.
- **[Checkable]** The prose does not always match the exhibits:
  - p. 5 says "Eighty-five percent have good quality lighting, and 75% have a good appearance rating." Figure 1a (p. 5) and the pooled Table 1 values show the reverse: appearance 0.85, lighting 0.75.
  - p. 2 gives the ventilation gap as "25 percentage points," while Table 1 and p. 6 give 25.9.
  - p. 12 says the decomposition controls for school "type," which is not among the Table 2 covariates.
- **[Checkable]** Several supporting claims can be verified only through the appendix or the authors, and I could not check them:
  - the exact BCS items and cutpoints (Appendix Table A1; p. 4), and the Likert distributions that justify binarization (Table A2; note 5);
  - the Model 1 and Model 3 sensitivity results, including the claim that property taxes fall "from roughly 30% to roughly 20%" (Appendix Figure A8, Table A13; p. 11);
  - the SEM/latent-factor robustness (Tables A11–A12; note 11, which reports RMSEA = .054 but no software or item loadings);
  - the index SDs of "0.14 to 0.17" (p. 8), which appear in no main-text table.
  - Note 4's claim that the 2,473-school sample "shows no evidence of systematic differences from the full universe" (p. 13) cites no exhibit.
  - Group means of the fiscal covariates, and the group-specific regression coefficients, are not reported in the main text. The main text also cites no appendix table containing them.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- The internal arithmetic is solid, and a reader can trust it: Table 1 differences and index averages, the Table 2 sums, and Figure 3 percentages all recompute from the printed numbers. That is not an independent check. None of the core estimates can be re-derived without the NYSED-provided BCS file, and no route to that file is documented.
- Anyone replicating should ask the authors, or NYSED's Office of Facilities Planning, for: the BCS extract and item crosswalk; the building-to-school aggregation rule; the fiscal-year and denominator definitions; and a sample-flow table explaining 2,371 (Table 1) vs. 2,352 (text) vs. 1,440/1,459 (Table 2). Absent these, expect the sample to differ.
- Treat the per-covariate split in Figure 3 as specification-dependent. The printed rows omit an unreported constant/intercept term worth about 84% of the gap, and the omitted categories are unstated. The property-tax endowment term alone is 0.0425/0.0830 ≈ 51% of the gap (Table 2). Whether one quotes that or the 30% "combined" figure depends on a presentation choice the paper does not defend. A replicator should run `oaxaca` with and without `normalize()` on the school-level and locale dummies and compare.

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: a reporting omission, not an error in the paper.*

- Re-estimate the Table 2 SEs clustered by district before relying on the marginal finance contributions (e.g., donations, state aid in the environmental index).
- Treat the Model 1–3 sensitivity claim (p. 11), the SEM robustness (note 11), and the representativeness claim (note 4) as unverified until the supplement is examined. They cannot be checked from the article.
- Before citing the swimming-pool gap (p. 7) or the appearance and lighting rates (p. 5), check them against Table 1 and Figure 1. The printed star and prose appear inconsistent with the tabulated values.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Data availability.* The article names five sources (pp. 3–4) with enough specificity to identify them. For four of them (CCD, MEPS, Comptroller district finances, and ACS EdTab 2013–2017), my understanding is that the files are publicly obtainable. This is a judgment, with high confidence for CCD, MEPS, and EdTab and moderately high confidence for the Comptroller data. The central outcome data, the 2015 BCS, are different. The paper describes the survey's legal basis and administration (p. 3) and thanks NYSED's Office of Facilities Planning for providing the data (p. 12). It says nothing about whether other researchers can obtain the same extract, under what terms, or in what form. Restricted or agency-provided data are a legitimate constraint, and the absence of a public file is not itself a failing. But for a 2026 article, journal-era norms call for at least a data availability statement and an access pathway, and the paper has neither. It also provides no code, no deposited package, and no Stata version. Naming `oaxaca` (note 9) is helpful but does not substitute for any of these.

*Sample construction.* The weakest link is the sample flow. The text gives a clean funnel (2,926 → 2,875 → 2,473 → 2,352), and the school-level breakdown sums correctly to 2,352 (p. 4). But the main descriptive table has 2,371 schools, and the decomposition has 1,440 where the two groups compared hold 1,459. No exhibit explains either gap, or the 121 schools lost in merging. The "cleaning" behind the 2,473 figure is not described either. That matters because the BCS is administered at the building level (p. 3), the analysis is at the school level, and the paper gives no aggregation rule. The note 4 claim that the analytic sample is representative is asserted without a cited exhibit.

*Variable and specification transparency.* Measurement is the most reproducible part of the paper. Table 1 reports every item that enters each index, and the unweighted item means reproduce the index rows exactly, so a replicator can confirm the averaging scheme. Two things remain opaque from the main text: the item wording and Likert cutpoints (deferred to Appendix Tables A1–A2, which I could not check) and the coding of condition items for schools without the facility. The finance covariates are thinly documented. The paper gives no fiscal year, per-pupil denominator, or revenue account definitions, and it says nothing about how district-level dollars map to schools. The decomposition is well specified in form: the equations on p. 4 fix the NW-coefficient reference, the variable list is clear, and robust SEs are stated. It is under-specified in its details: omitted categories, `oaxaca` options, weighting, and the constant term. The unreported constant matters in practice. For the overall index, the listed coefficient rows sum to −0.0095 against a reported coefficients component of 0.0603, so most of the "coefficients" share the paper emphasizes (p. 8) sits in a term readers never see. Dummy-variable coefficient effects also depend on the omitted category unless normalized. Figure 3's percentages are therefore arithmetically faithful to Table 2 but not uniquely determined by the paper's verbal specification.

*Results reporting and verifiability.* The paper is generous with point estimates and SEs for the decomposition, and its exhibits are internally consistent to a degree that builds some confidence in the pipeline. Figure 1 matches pooled Table 1. Table 1's aggregates match its items. Table 2's summary rows add up, and Figure 3 follows from Table 2. There are also small but concrete inconsistencies: two Table 1 significance marks that the reported proportions cannot support, the appearance/lighting swap in the p. 5 prose, and "25" vs. "25.9" percentage points for ventilation. None of these changes the substantive picture, but they are the kind of error a deposited script would catch. The student-weighted exposure results (Figure 2) cannot be checked at all from the article. There are no SEs in the figure, the bootstrap cluster is unstated, and the full table is in the appendix. The robustness claims that support the paper's interpretation (Models 1–3, the SEM indices) are available only in supplementary material I could not access.

*Overall calibration.* I rate this **Weak** rather than Adequate. The central decomposition's inputs (the BCS extract, and the finance variables as constructed) cannot be obtained or rebuilt from the article, the published sample counts do not reconcile, and there is no data availability statement or code. So verification beyond internal arithmetic is not currently possible. The rating is not Insufficient because the analysis is understandable, the specification is largely stated, and the internal consistency checks mostly pass. My confidence is moderate, not high, because the unseen supplement (especially Tables A1, A2, and A13) may close some of the measurement and sensitivity gaps. It would not close the data-access, code, or sample-reconciliation gaps.
